issues.subcategory: contradictory SESOI specification
issues.description: The equivalence region is stated as δ = .27 in one paragraph and then explicitly changed to δ = |.11| two paragraphs later, with the latter described as the actual analytic decision. These are substantially different values, and it is unclear which will actually be used. This is a critical ambiguity for a registered report where the equivalence bounds determine the primary inferential conclusions for hypotheses 2b and 3b.
issues.quote: We will use the Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression (Counsell & Cribbie, 2015), with an equivalence region based on the smallest effect size of interest (SESOI) of δ= .27.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent Cohen's d for same effect
issues.description: The same effect from Grubbs, Lee, et al. (2020), with identical ΔR² = .012 and f² = .016, is reported as Cohen's d = .22 in one location and Cohen's d = .25 in another. Only one of these can be correct. Additionally, using d = 2√f² gives d = 2√.016 = .253, which matches neither .22 nor .25 exactly, though .25 is closer.
issues.quote: ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020

issues.subcategory: incorrect Cohen's d conversion
issues.description: For the first reported effect (Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020), ΔR² = .014, f² = .020, is reported with Cohen's d = .24. However, using the standard conversion d = 2√f², this yields d = 2√.020 = .283, not .24. This is a non-trivial discrepancy that affects the characterization of prior effect sizes.
issues.quote: ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen's d = .24, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020

issues.subcategory: PGSI response scale mismatch between text and supplementals
issues.description: The methods section describes the PGSI as using a '4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always),' which matches the validated instrument. However, the supplemental materials show response values of Never (0), Sometimes (2), Most of the time (4), Almost Always (5). These are non-standard values that do not correspond to the validated PGSI scoring, would alter total scores and clinical cut-offs, and directly contradict the methods text.
issues.quote: on a 4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always). Responses will be averaged.

issues.subcategory: BPS response scale mismatch between text and supplementals
issues.description: The methods section describes the Brief Pornography Screen as using a 'three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often)' with summed responses. However, the supplemental materials show response values of Never (0), Occasionally (2), Very Often (4). This would change the maximum possible score from 10 to 20, fundamentally altering the psychometric properties and clinical interpretation of the scale.
issues.quote: reporting the frequency they have experienced certain behaviors...on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed.

issues.subcategory: frequency scale numbering inconsistency
issues.description: The pornography and gambling sections describe frequency as measured on a scale from 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day), but the supplemental materials and the ASSIST section describe the same scale as 0 (never) to 5 (more than once per day). This inconsistency affects whether non-use is coded as 0 or 1, which matters for the interaction terms (as it changes the zero-point of the variable) and affects interpretation of centered variables.
issues.quote: participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)

issues.subcategory: construct mismatch within methods section
issues.description: The analytic plan introduction describes the key interaction as 'moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action,' but the actual operationalization throughout the rest of the manuscript is the interaction of moral disapproval with frequency of the behavior. Severity of consequences and behavioral frequency are distinct constructs.
issues.quote: Central to the proposed study is the measurement of moral incongruence as the interaction of moral disapproval of an action with severity of consequences from the action.

issues.subcategory: biased oversample affecting gambling analyses
issues.description: The sports-wagering oversample (n=1,500) is combined with the nationally representative sample for gambling analyses (effective N = 3,325). This oversample was recruited specifically for having recent wagering history and likely has systematically different moral attitudes toward gambling, gambling frequency distributions, and gambling problem severity than the general population. Combining these samples inflates the gambling subsample in non-representative ways and could bias the moral incongruence interaction test for gambling specifically—one of the key hypothesis tests. No weighting or analytic strategy to account for this sampling design is described.
issues.quote: Gambling | 73% (national sample) 100% (sports-betting oversample) | 3,325

issues.subcategory: non-parallel outcome measures across behaviors
issues.description: Pornography and gambling are assessed using validated, dedicated instruments (BPS and PGSI respectively), while all substance use problems are assessed using modified NIDA-ASSIST items that have been altered from their original form. This asymmetry means the pornography analysis uses a measure specifically designed and validated to capture compulsive pornography use, while substance analyses use a general screening tool. Differences in findings could reflect measurement properties rather than true differences in moral incongruence effects.
issues.quote: In addition to the modified NIDA-ASSIST items listed above, self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography will be assessed using the Brief Pornography Screen

issues.subcategory: averaging items on incompatible scales
issues.description: The NIDA-ASSIST problematic use composite averages three frequency items scored 0–5 with two items scored on a 3-point scale of 0, 3, and 6. Averaging items with such different ranges and metrics creates a composite where the dichotomous-like items (with values 0, 3, 6) have disproportionate influence and the resulting average has no clear psychometric interpretation. The two non-frequency items effectively have a range of 0–6 while the frequency items have a range of 0–5, and the non-frequency items have only 3 possible values creating a highly non-normal distribution.
issues.quote: Participants will also respond to two questions...on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be averaged

issues.subcategory: no multiple comparison correction for primary analyses
issues.description: The study proposes 8 moderation analyses as primary tests, including both standard significance tests and equivalence tests. No correction for multiple comparisons is described for the primary hypothesis tests. For a registered report, this represents undisclosed analytic flexibility, particularly since the key claim (moral incongruence is unique to pornography) depends on finding significance for pornography but not for other behaviors. The familywise error rate across 8 tests at α = .05 is approximately .34.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.subcategory: moral disapproval not equivalent across behaviors
issues.description: A single item asking if a behavior is 'morally wrong' may capture fundamentally different constructs across behaviors. For illicit drugs, 'moral disapproval' likely conflates moral judgment with legal/health concerns and may have near-ceiling values among users, creating restriction of range. For alcohol, a socially normative substance, moral disapproval captures a more purely moral stance. For pornography, moral disapproval is closely tied to religious/sexual values. These construct differences mean that a non-significant interaction for substances could reflect measurement artifacts rather than genuine differences in how moral incongruence operates.
issues.quote: we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement "I believe that using ________ is morally wrong" on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: severely underpowered subgroups
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that prescription drug misuse (estimated n=140, power=.301) and illicit substance use (estimated n=240-480, power=.472-.764) analyses will be substantially underpowered to detect the target effect size. A power of .301 means there is only a 30% chance of detecting a true effect, making the equivalence test for prescription drugs largely uninterpretable. The proposed fallback using a larger equivalence region changes the research question from 'is this effect null?' to 'is this effect smaller than the pornography effect?'—a fundamentally different hypothesis.
issues.quote: Prescription Drug Misuse | 3.5% | 140 | .057 | .301

issues.subcategory: confirmation bias in hypothesis framing
issues.description: The introduction explicitly states the study has 'a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors,' and the hypotheses predict null effects for gambling and substances. For a registered report aiming to adjudicate between competing theoretical positions, this framing introduces an a priori commitment to one outcome that may bias interpretation of ambiguous results.
issues.quote: with a specific goal of demonstrating that moral incongruence is unique in predicting compulsive sexual behaviors

issues.subcategory: cross-sectional design with causal language
issues.description: The study is cross-sectional, yet the theoretical framework and hypotheses imply causal direction (moral incongruence 'predicts' or 'contributes to' feelings of addiction). The cross-sectional interaction between moral disapproval and frequency cannot establish that moral incongruence causally produces feelings of addiction, as opposed to addiction experiences generating moral distress. While acknowledged briefly in limitations, the hypotheses and theoretical implications sections use consistently causal framing.
issues.quote: moral incongruence regarding pornography use will predict self-reported feelings of addiction

issues.subcategory: unclear number and specification of primary analyses
issues.description: Table 1 shows that both pornography and gambling have two outcome measures each (validated instrument + modified NIDA-ASSIST), yielding 5 + 2 + 2 = 9 possible analyses. The text states 8 analyses but it is unclear which specific combinations constitute these 8. Whether NIDA-ASSIST gambling is included as a primary analysis or not is never specified, yet this choice could substantially affect conclusions about moral incongruence in gambling.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 8 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest

issues.subcategory: different time frames across outcome measures
issues.description: The BPS measures experiences in the 'last 6 months,' the PGSI measures the 'last 12 months,' the NIDA-ASSIST problematic use items reference 'the past three months,' and the two additional NIDA-ASSIST items have no specified time frame ('ever'). These different recall periods make cross-behavior comparisons problematic, as the sensitivity to detect associations may differ across measures simply due to temporal coverage.
issues.quote: In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you in regards to your use of pornography?

issues.subcategory: modified NIDA-ASSIST not validated for pornography/gambling
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that including pornography and gambling within the NIDA-ASSIST framework 'is not currently validated for gambling or pornography,' yet propose using these scores as outcome variables. While they include validated measures as well, one of the 8 primary analyses appears to use the NIDA-ASSIST pornography items as an outcome to define the equivalence comparison region, making an unvalidated measure central to the inferential framework.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: overly optimistic assumptions about data quality
issues.description: The authors assume no data quality issues and no missing data based on YouGov's proprietary processes. This is unrealistic for a survey of this length and complexity. No contingency plan for handling missing data (e.g., multiple imputation, listwise deletion) is described, nor are attention check items mentioned. For a registered report, the absence of a missing data strategy is a notable gap.
issues.quote: we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: underspecified robustness procedures
issues.description: The analytic plan states that when regression assumptions are violated, 'we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.' The nature of these supplemental analyses is not specified (e.g., robust regression, bootstrapping, transformation). For a registered report, leaving the choice of alternative analytic technique entirely open creates a researcher degree of freedom.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate.

issues.subcategory: restriction of range in moral disapproval for certain substances
issues.description: For illicit drug use and prescription drug misuse, the base rate of moral disapproval is likely very high (most people believe illegal drug use is morally wrong). Among the small subset of users, this could create either ceiling effects (if users still disapprove) or severe restriction of range (if only low-disapproval individuals use), both of which would attenuate the interaction effect and bias the equivalence test toward finding null effects, consistent with the authors' hypothesis.
issues.quote: I believe that using illegal/illicit drugs is morally wrong

issues.subcategory: supplemental heavy drinking item mislabeled
issues.description: For men, the question asks about 'more than 5 drinks on one occasion' but the response row label says 'More than four drinks (1).' This contradicts the question stem and incorrectly uses the women's threshold (4 drinks) in the men's version. The '(1)' notation is also unexplained.
issues.quote:
IF GENDER = MAN
In the past year, how often have you had more than 5 drinks on one occasion?
...More than four drinks (1)

issues.subcategory: U.S.-only sample for cross-cultural construct
issues.description: The study aims to draw general conclusions about whether moral incongruence is unique to sexual behavior, but uses only a U.S. sample. Moral attitudes toward pornography, gambling, and substance use vary substantially across cultures. The authors acknowledge this in limitations but the hypotheses and planned conclusions are framed in universal terms.
issues.quote: Although a nationally representative sample in the U.S. is better than convenience sampling methods, such a sample represents only one broad cultural context in which these hypotheses could be tested.

issues.subcategory: conflation of standardized β with Cohen's δ in equivalence test
issues.description: The authors set their equivalence region δ equal to a standardized regression coefficient β (= .11), treating these as interchangeable metrics. However, standardized regression coefficients (partial effects controlling for other predictors) and Cohen's δ are not the same effect size metric. The Anderson-Hauck equivalence test for regression as described by Counsell & Cribbie (2015) uses standardized coefficients, but the manuscript switches between calling the SESOI 'δ' (implying Cohen's d) and equating it with β values, creating confusion about what metric is actually being used for the equivalence bounds.
issues.quote: we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11

issues.subcategory: religiousness measured by panel data potentially stale
issues.description: Age, gender, and religiousness are assessed using pre-existing YouGov panel data rather than measured contemporaneously with the study. Panel data may be months or years old, and religiousness can change over time. No information is provided about when these items were administered or how current the data are, which could introduce measurement error in a key covariate.
issues.quote: Age, gender, and religiousness will be assessed using panel data provided by YouGov (i.e., not as a part of our survey).

issues.subcategory: fallback equivalence region uses obtained estimate
issues.description: The contingency plan for underpowered analyses redefines the equivalence region using the lower bound of the 95% CI from the pornography interaction effect obtained in the same study. This is circular: the equivalence bound for one analysis depends on the outcome of another analysis in the same dataset, which introduces data-dependent analytic decisions. The choice of the lower bound of the CI (rather than, e.g., the point estimate) is also a researcher degree of freedom.
issues.quote: we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.subcategory: filter question excludes non-users from moral disapproval analysis
issues.description: The text states 'Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use,' but also states 'we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.' This is contradictory. If only users complete problematic use measures, then the moral incongruence interaction is only tested among users, which restricts range on frequency and potentially inflates the interaction. If everyone completes everything, then zeros on problematic use for non-users create floor effects.
issues.quote: Only participants who endorse past-year use will complete further measures of problematic use...we will administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to all participants in the sample.

issues.subcategory: no specification of how non-binary gender will be handled
issues.description: Gender is coded as binary (1 = male, 0 = not-male) for analytic purposes, but no mention is made of how non-binary, transgender, or other gender-diverse participants will be categorized, or whether the YouGov panel offers non-binary gender options. Collapsing diverse gender identities into 'not-male' may be inappropriate and could introduce heterogeneity within this category.
issues.quote: gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.subcategory: asymmetric theoretical treatment of pornography vs. other behaviors
issues.description: The theoretical framework extensively develops why moral incongruence should predict problematic pornography use but offers relatively thin theoretical reasoning for why it should NOT predict substance or gambling problems. The prediction that moral incongruence is unique to pornography is primarily justified by the ICD-11 diagnostic caveat and prior empirical findings, rather than by a clear theoretical mechanism explaining why morality would interact with frequency for pornography but not for gambling or substances. Without such a mechanism, null results for other behaviors may reflect measurement differences rather than true theoretical distinctions.
issues.quote: However, morality may influence a wide range of human behaviors, including addictive behavior processes, and discrepancies between moral beliefs about a behavior and actual engagement with a behavior are likely present in a variety of addictions.
